about: Black neighborhoods and districts of Atlanta, 1865-1945, as the sources give them. Each entry is one label at one point; the point is where the place is centred or described, NOT a boundary, and the layer draws no outline. start/end are only what a source states. A place with no stated start year has start null and is hidden until 'undated' is switched on. kind: black = documented as a Black community; mixed = documented as mixed. Sources are the book's own Setting Guide (chapters/0003-atlanta-setting-guide/05-neighborhoods.md), which carries its own citations, plus the pages named in each entry. Wikipedia is a secondary source and is cited as such.

places.name: Shermantown
places.date_source: Setting Guide, Shermantown: named for the general whose army burned the city 'a year earlier'; it held 2,486 people by 1870 (citing Wikipedia 'Racial segregation in Atlanta' and the AJC)
places.location: The Setting Guide places it in the low ground of the Fourth Ward, 'in what is now the Sweet Auburn area, around the street then still called Wheat Street' (Atlanta History Center via DLG), and counts more than a hundred Black-owned businesses 'around Edgewood Avenue' by 1910 (GSU, Histories of Our Streets). The point is the midpoint of Auburn and Edgewood at Courtland, between the two descriptions; it is not a boundary.
places.note: The name 'fades into the Fourth Ward' by the 1900s (Setting Guide); no end year. Not the Shermantown at Stone Mountain village, which is a different place. canon/places.yml's shermantown entry says 'East of Oakland Cemetery', which none of these sources say; the Setting Guide's location is used here.

places.name: Auburn Avenue
places.date_source: Wheat Street Baptist Church was founded in 1869 (SAH Archipedia, via the Setting Guide); 'Black congregations were already there' (Setting Guide). Wheat Street renamed Auburn Avenue in 1893 at white petitioners' request (Georgia Encyclopedia, Auburn Avenue; canon/timeline.yml)
places.location: Auburn at Butler Street, the middle of the stretch between Courtland and Jackson where the Setting Guide's churches and businesses stood.
places.note: East of Jackson Street the avenue was 'a mostly white, middle-class residential street before 1900' (NPS Historic Resource Study, via the Setting Guide), and Black businesses moved onto it after 1906 (Georgia Encyclopedia: Atlanta). The start year here is the churches', not the business district's. John Wesley Dobbs is credited with the name 'Sweet Auburn' (Wikipedia, 'Sweet Auburn'), with no year given, so that name is not used.

places.name: Darktown
places.date_source: No source gives a start or end year. Wikipedia ('Darktown') quotes a 1930s description (Silver and Moeser, The Separate City, p. 130)
places.location: Wikipedia ('Darktown', citing Calt, Barrelhouse Words, p. 69) says it 'stretched from Peachtree Street and Collins Street (now Courtland Street), past Butler Ave. (now Jesse Hill Jr. Ave.) to Jackson Street', in the blocks above Auburn Avenue. The point is the midpoint of Auburn at Courtland and Auburn at Jackson; the north edge is not stated.
places.note: An outsiders' name, used in canon/places.yml for Houston Street and in the 1930s by white observers as an insult ('hell-hole of squalor...'); the sources do not say what residents called it, or whether it was ever a name they used. Shown only when 'undated' is switched on, because no year is documented.

places.name: Summerhill
places.date_source: Settled 1865, one of two settlements William Jennings laid out; named by an early Black settler, Armsted Bailey Sr. (Wikipedia 'Summerhill, Atlanta'; AUC Woodruff Library exhibit, via the Setting Guide)
places.location: Just south of the Capitol (Setting Guide). Wikipedia gives no boundary streets; Allen Temple AME began as Wood's Chapel in 1866 and the school at Richardson and Martin Streets dates to 1867 (Wikipedia, no inline source).
places.note: Black families founded it; Jewish families lived there from the 1880s, and one count puts two-thirds of Atlanta's Jewish residents there in 1911 (Setting Guide; Wikipedia). It was cleared in part for the stadium after 1945 (Wikipedia), which is outside this layer's years.

places.name: Mechanicsville
places.date_source: 'Mechanicsville was established in 1870' (Wikipedia 'Mechanicsville, Atlanta', no inline source); 'dating to about 1870' (Setting Guide)
places.location: South of downtown, its southwest edge the Southern Railway's tracks, across which lies Pittsburg (Setting Guide; Wikipedia).
places.note: Mixed: 'working class blacks and middle class whites' (Wikipedia, no date); one of the Black neighborhoods that took shape in the 1870s (Wikipedia 'Racial segregation in Atlanta', via the Setting Guide). No source gives when it became majority Black.

places.name: Pittsburg
places.date_source: Founded in 1883 on 554 acres by Black laborers beside the Pegram rail shops (Saporta Report; Pittsburgh Yards; Wikipedia 'Pittsburgh, Atlanta', citing Laura Ferguson, Atlanta INtown, June 2007)
places.location: South and southwest of downtown, across the Southern Railway's tracks from Mechanicsville; McDaniel Street is its main street (Setting Guide).
places.note: Spelled 'Pittsburg' in the period sources, 'Pittsburgh' today (canon/places.yml; Setting Guide). Predominantly Black (Wikipedia).

places.name: Vine City
places.date_source: 'Settled at the end of the 1800s by large land owners' and 'a predominantly African-American residential area was established' (Wikipedia 'Vine City', no inline source and no year); Alonzo Herndon built his home there in 1910 (same, citing Vine City Health and Housing Ministry). 1900 is a rounding of 'the end of the 1800s'
places.location: West of downtown, south of Simpson Road, near the Atlanta University Center (Wikipedia; Setting Guide).
places.note: 'By the 1920s-1940s' Black residents were moving north across Simpson Road despite violence and bombings (Wikipedia, citing the English Avenue redevelopment plan). Eagan Homes and Herndon Homes opened in 1941 (Wikipedia, no inline source).

places.name: Beaver Slide
places.date_source: 'Documented as early as 1882' (Wikipedia 'Beaver Slide'). The area was cleared in 1934, the first shacks dynamited on September 29, 1934 (canon/bible.md, 'Techwood and Beaver Slide, 1935', citing Ickes and the Atlanta Housing Authority); land for University Homes was acquired in May 1934 and construction began that September (Georgia Historical Society marker, via search). University Homes opened April 15, 1937, 1938 in some sources. 1935 is when the ground stood cleared
places.location: Near Atlanta University (Wikipedia); canon/places.yml names Parsons, Elm, Maher, Dora, Greensferry and Lawshe Streets for the University Homes site.
places.note: Wikipedia calls it an 'African American slum area'; the Setting Guide calls it 'a slum of rough houses'. The name's origin is disputed (a police chief named Beavers, 'Snake Nation' renamed). Who was displaced, and where they went, is unsettled in the canon (open items).

places.name: Atlanta University
places.date_source: 'Atlanta University dates to 1865'; Spelman 1881 (Seminary 1884, College 1924); Morehouse took its name in 1913 (Westside Future Fund, via the Setting Guide)
places.lonlat_basis: OpenStreetMap place:neighbourhood node, Atlanta University Center (via Nominatim).
places.location: West of downtown, past the rail yards (Setting Guide).
places.note: The cluster of Black colleges, the largest concentration of educated Black Atlanta (Setting Guide). Clark and Gammon were at Brownsville until 1929 (see 'brownsville').

places.name: Brownsville
places.date_source: Grew around Clark University and Gammon Theological Seminary on land Methodist bishop Gilbert Haven bought in 1877 (EJI and Fulton County Remembrance Coalition marker, via the Setting Guide); Clark moved there in 1883 (Wikipedia 'South Atlanta'); in 1887 Clark formed the South Atlanta Land Improvement Company to develop 50 acres as a Black suburb; about 2,000 people lived there by 1904 (marker)
places.lonlat_basis: Wikipedia 'South Atlanta' infobox coordinates (33°42′54″N 84°23′6″W); South Atlanta was 'originally known as Brownsville'.
places.location: About two miles south of downtown and outside the city limits (Setting Guide). Wikipedia's South Atlanta boundaries: the railroad and Chosewood Park to the northeast, Turman Street to the south.
places.note: September 1906: residents armed to protect their homes, a shootout and the militia's arrests followed (Georgia Encyclopedia, 1906 Massacre). In 1929 Atlanta University, Spelman and Morehouse moved to the West Side, which the City's planning document calls unfortunate for the neighborhood.

places.name: Reynoldstown
places.date_source: Wikipedia's infobox gives 'Built 1865' and the text says it was 'originally settled after the American Civil War by freed slaves who were employed by the railroad' (tagged 'citation needed'); Wikipedia 'Reynoldstown'
places.location: East of downtown, between the rail line, Memorial Drive, Pearl Street and Moreland Avenue (Wikipedia).
places.note: Named, it is believed, for Madison and Sarah Reynolds, among the first ex-slaves there; annexed by Atlanta in 1909 (Wikipedia). It 'continued to thrive and prosper until the 1950s' (same). Thin sourcing: the one reliable fact is the annexation.

places.name: Buttermilk Bottom
places.date_source: No source gives when it formed. 'Most of Buttermilk Bottom was razed in the 1960s' (Wikipedia 'Buttermilk Bottom', citing Keating, Atlanta: Race, Class and Urban Expansion, p. 106), outside this layer's years
places.lonlat_basis: Wikipedia: 'centered on the area where the Atlanta Civic Center now stands'; the point is the Civic Center's OpenStreetMap building (via Nominatim).
places.location: In the Old Fourth Ward, low ground toward Piedmont Avenue (canon/places.yml).
places.note: Described as 'a slum area, having unpaved streets and no electricity' (Wikipedia, no date). Shown only when 'undated' is switched on. canon/places.yml calls the 1907 low ground 'later Buttermilk Bottom'; whether the name was in use then is not sourced here.
